quiz.title: Smart Study & Choosing eBooks Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on picking good study eBooks and studying them well. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Choosing study eBooks and effective study habits

questions.q: Before buying a study eBook, which check tells you most about its quality?
options: A preview or sample of a real chapter
The cover design
The number of pages
The price alone
questions.explanation: A sample chapter shows the actual explanations, examples and worked answers, which reveals quality far better than the cover, length or price.

questions.q: You have read a chapter and closed the book. What is the strongest way to check you actually learned it?
options: Re-read the chapter twice more
Cover the page and recall the main points from memory
Highlight the key lines again
Skim the summary
questions.explanation: Active recall, retrieving the ideas from memory without looking, builds far stronger, longer-lasting learning than re-reading or highlighting.

options: Studying one subject for many hours in a row
Leaving wide spaces in your notes
Revisiting the same material over several days with gaps between sessions
Studying only the night before a test
questions.explanation: Spaced practice spreads short review sessions across days. The gaps force recall and beat one long cram session for memory.

questions.q: An eBook includes end-of-chapter practice questions with answer keys. Why does that matter?
options: It makes the file larger
It looks more professional
It replaces the need to read the chapter
It lets you test yourself and find gaps before an exam
questions.explanation: Practice tests turn passive reading into self-testing. Checking answers shows exactly which topics still need work, well before the real exam.

questions.q: Which is a realistic, useful reading goal for a study eBook?
options: Read one chapter and do its questions, three evenings a week
Finish the whole book in one sitting
Read only when you feel motivated
Read every book on the topic before starting practice
questions.explanation: A specific, repeatable goal tied to a schedule is achievable and measurable. Vague or all-at-once goals tend to stall.

questions.q: Two eBooks cover the same syllabus. One lists no author or sources; the other names its author and cites the syllabus. Which is safer to trust?
options: The one with no author, since it is simpler
Whichever is cheaper
The one that names its author and cites the syllabus
It makes no difference
questions.explanation: A named author and clear sources signal accountability and let you judge credibility, an idea Google calls E-E-A-T. Anonymous, unsourced material is riskier.

questions.q: You keep forgetting a topic no matter how often you re-read it. What should you try next?
options: Re-read it a fifth time
Skip it and hope it is not on the test
Copy the whole section by hand
Explain it aloud in your own words, as if teaching someone
questions.explanation: Explaining a topic in your own words, sometimes called the teach-back or Feynman approach, exposes the exact gaps that silent re-reading hides.

questions.q: What is the best use of an answer key while practising?
options: Copy the answers straight into your notes
Attempt each question first, then check the key and review your mistakes
Read the answers before trying the questions
Ignore it entirely
questions.explanation: The value is in attempting first, then using the key to confirm and to understand why any answer was wrong. Reading answers first removes the retrieval that makes practice work.

faq.q: How do I judge whether a lesser-known eBook is worth reading?
faq.a: Look past the download count. Read a sample chapter, check that it names an author and its sources, and see whether it includes practice questions or an answer key. A clear preview tells you more about quality than reviews or price.

faq.q: Are lesser-known eBooks less reliable than bestsellers?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Popularity measures reach, not accuracy. A well-sourced eBook by a named author can be more useful for your exact syllabus than a famous title written for a general audience. Judge each book on its content, not its fame.

faq.q: What is the most effective way to study from an eBook?
faq.a: Read a chapter, then close it and recall the main points from memory. This active recall, spread over several short sessions rather than one long cram, fixes ideas far better than re-reading or highlighting.

faq.q: How do practice tests inside an eBook help me learn?
faq.a: Self-testing shows you exactly which topics you have not yet mastered, so you can review them before an exam instead of discovering the gap during it. Always attempt a question first, then check the answer key and study any mistakes.
